episodes.201222: Strong to severe thunderstorms, including miniature supercells, developed during the late afternoon and early evening hours before weakening and pushing east into Georgia after midnight. The thunderstorms produced damaging winds and a tornado in north central portions of Alabama. Isolated flash flooding occurred as well.
episodes.201223: Strong thunderstorms (including mini-supercells) developed during the late afternoon and evening hours in southern middle Tennessee before weakening and pushing out of the area overnight. Damaging winds to 50 mph occurred in some areas.
episodes.201275: A complex severe weather setup evolved overnight as a line of storms moved into northwest Webb County, tracking east-southeast through South Texas into the early morning hours. The main drivers of this event included a slow-moving mid-level circulation (MCV) originating from storms over southeast New Mexico, and an approaching upper-level shortwave that was set to enhance thunderstorm activity overnight. The presence of rich moisture, steep lapse rates, and sufficient upper-level flow created favorable conditions for damaging winds.
episodes.201276: Heavy rain and isolated flooding developed across central and south Texas during the early morning hours as deep convection expanded across the region. A very moist and unstable atmosphere with PWATs near 1.75 and MLCAPE around 2000 J/kg fueled thunderstorms capable of producing intense rainfall rates of 1-2/hour. These storms were largely driven by outflows, with limited low-level shear. As thunderstorms merged and propagated eastward, aided by steep lapse rates and minimal CIN, many areas saw at least an inch of rain, with higher totals in spots. While most locations remained below flash flood guidance thresholds, the heavier downpours caused some localized flooding.
episodes.201292: Upslope easterly flow and higher surface moisture across the central mountain chain and eastern New Mexico combined with daytime heating to result in the development of showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. One of these thunderstorms produced pea to penny size hail in Des Moines. A backdoor front pushed through eastern New Mexico on May 29th replenishing surface moisture and providing extra lift for the development of another round of showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours across this part of the state. One thunderstorm dropped penny size hail in rural eastern Lincoln County for a brief period of time. Shower and thunderstorm activity tapered off shortly after sunset with the loss of daytime heating.||Key Word: Hail.
episodes.201411: A low pressure system brought a warm front and then cold front into West Virginia on May  28th. The cold front became stationary and then weakened over the area later that night. While rainfall amounts for the 28th were mainly less than an inch and a half, a couple of inches fell over localized portions of Harrison and Taylor Counties. Rainfall from the previous day had also helped to saturate the ground, making flooding easier to occur. In Harrison and Taylor Counties, several roadways flooded and at least one water rescue occurred in the midst of the heavy rain.
episodes.201512: Slow moving thunderstorms produced isolated areas of flash flooding.
episodes.201514: Showers and thunderstorms along a coastal trough began training over the same small area leading to flash flooding.
episodes.201614: A cold front tracked across the waters of Eastern North Carolina bringing widespread rain and isolated thunderstorms to the inland and coastal waters. A few isolated thunderstorms became strong in nature impacting portions of the Pamlico Sound on the morning of the twenty-eighth. Strong wind gusts were the primary hazard within the strongest storms.
episodes.201844: A surface low tracked across northern Iowa and while this produced only light sprinkles, it did produce enough low level stretching for several funnel clouds to be reported across northern and central Iowa. The 0-3 km CAPE at the time of the reports was analyzed around 75-100 J/kg.
episodes.202160: With an approaching low and dynamically primed atmosphere, storms were able to develop and take advantage of ample moisture. The event began with fairly isolated supercells moving primarily eastward before a line of storms took over descending from the northwest. The storms produced numerous hail reports and a funnel cloud.
episodes.202174: An upper-level shortwave trough moved across a stationary front that was stretched across Central Texas. Some of these storms moved into South-Central Texas producing damaging wind gusts and large hail. There were also a few reports of heavy rain leading to flash flooding.
episodes.202202: In the afternoon of the 28th, a scattered line of storms formed in northeastern Colorado and moved to the south-southeast. As these storms passed over Burlington, nickel sized hail was reported.
episodes.202203: In the afternoon of the 28th, a scattered line of storms formed in northeastern Colorado and moved to the south-southeast into western Kansas. As these storms passed over Lydia, quarter sized hail was reported.
episodes.202272: A trough passing over the region, a nearby dryline, and upslope surface flow allowed for the development of scattered thunderstorms across Southeast New Mexico and West Texas. Large hail was reported in Brewster County in/near the higher elevation. Some strong winds were also measured that evening. High non-thunderstorm winds were also reported in the Guadalupe Mountains overnight as the trough/Pacific front moved through.
episodes.202273: A trough passing over the region, a nearby dryline, and upslope surface flow allowed for the development of scattered thunderstorms across Southeast New Mexico and West Texas. Large hail was reported in Brewster County in/near the higher elevation. Some strong winds were also measured that evening. High non-thunderstorm winds were also reported in the Guadalupe Mountains overnight as the trough/Pacific front moved through.
episodes.202322: A moist, deep, and increasing west-southwesterly flow led to a Gulf-dominant sea breeze regime and focused the corridor of scattered thunderstorm activity along the I-95 corridor and the First Coast during the afternoon and early evening. A few pulse severe storms produced gusty downburst winds.
episodes.202323: A moist, deep, and increasing west-southwesterly flow led to a Gulf-dominant sea breeze regime and focused the corridor of scattered thunderstorm activity along the I-95 corridor and the First Coast during the afternoon and early evening. A few pulse severe storms produced gusty downburst winds.
episodes.202608: A warm front lifted northward out of the Gulf across south Louisiana on May 28th. Lift provided by this boundary and accompanied low level moisture combined with strong daytime heating was able to a few severe thunderstorms. Those storms produced multiple severe wind gusts over local marine locations.
episodes.202609: A mid level disturbance embedded within southwest flow aloft created an environment of increased buoyancy. Ample instability was already in place across the region due to typical  early summer heat and increased low level moisture. A mix of severe and heavy rain impacts occurred as storms developed across the region.
episodes.202612: Upslope flow led to the development of a couple of isolated storms in the Davis Mountains. One storm moved into Brewster County, and produced dime size hail in Alpine.
episodes.202627: Scattered thunderstorms produced areas of gusty winds with several measurements in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.202972: The combination of an upper level area of low pressure and a stationary frontal boundary in the area, resulted in many rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms across west central Texas during late May. In addition, strong to locally extreme surface instability  along with strong vertical wind shear assisted with the development of severe thunderstorms. A few of the severe storms produced very large to giant size hail and a few tornadoes.
episodes.202991: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed along a subtle stationary boundary in the late afternoon and early evening hours across portions of southeast Georgia. A few of these storms became strong enough to produce damaging wind gusts.
episodes.202992: Multiple rounds of thunderstorms impacted the Atlantic coastal waters and adjacent coastline with strong wind gusts. The storms developed along a subtle stationary boundary with one round in the early morning hours followed by another round in the afternoon.
episodes.203099: Supercell thunderstorms moved southeast through the northeastern combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles on the 28th of May. These storms first produced large hail up to 1.75��� and wind gusts upwards of 87 mph, as well as a funnel cloud in Beaver County. As one of these storms moved into Lipscomb County in the Texas Panhandle, it produced hail that reached up to three inches in diameter.
episodes.203146: Towards the end of May, two more rounds of thunderstorms occurred, leading to a few isolated instances of severe weather. The first round involved a storm complex that tracked eastward from the Big Country into North and Central Texas. The second consisted of isolated thunderstorms linked to a weak cold front. In both instances, two reports of large hail were received.
episodes.203275: A dissipating front combined with upper-level energy to produce two lines of thunderstorms on successive mornings in late May 2025. The first situation, a decaying line of broken showers and a few thunderstorms, raced southward across the Lower Texas Gulf/Laguna Madre waters during the early morning of the 27th. On May 28th, a more intense squall line developed inland and gradually moved into the nearshore Gulf waters.  Gale-force wind gusts and torrential rainfall accompanied the second line in a few locations along the coast.
episodes.203285: A cold front moved into the region and stalled for multiple days while weak upper level disturbances triggered a few thunderstorms.
episodes.203292: A front moved into the region and stalled. This produced multiple days of unsettled weather along the coast.
episodes.203486: Increasing upper level moisture across eastern Utah and western Colorado led to the development of daily afternoon showers and thunderstorms over the higher terrain. However, dry surface levels meant that all precipitation falling out of this activity evaporated before reaching the ground, enhancing the convective outflow winds and allowing for stronger than expected gusts.
episodes.204272: Northwest flow was in place over the area and allowed for severe thunderstorms to develop across El Paso and Baca Counties.
episodes.204335: River flooding was noted along the Spring, White, Fourche LaFave, Arkansas, and Ouachita Rivers.
episodes.204773: Training thunderstorms produced some flash flooding over portions of northeastern Alabama during the morning hours on the 28th.
episodes.205177: A squall line moved through Mississippi on the 27th and produced wind damage.

A National Weather Service survey team concluded a long track microburst, associated with a supercell, caused sporadic, non-continuous wind damage in northwest Austin along the supercell's track. This consisted mainly of small to medium sized tree branches. Part of a gas station canopy collapsed onto two vehicles. Winds through this area were estimated at 55-75 mph.
A thunderstorm produced pea to quarter size hail in northeastern Austin.

A National Weather Service survey team concluded a long track microburst, associated with a supercell, occurred from central Austin, near the Hyde Park area, southeast to just east of the Austin Bergstrom International Airport. The length of the damage was approximately 10 miles long, with a path width ranging from one mile to a maximum of around 2.5 miles on the east side of Austin. Numerous trees and powerlines were damaged along the path. Large tree branches were snapped and a few trees uprooted that had shallow root systems. Minor shingle damage was observed on some homes. Maximum sustained winds were estimated to be between 65 and 85 mph. The Austin Bergstrom International Airport recorded a peak wind gust of 77 mph.

A National Weather Service survey team concluded a long track microburst, associated with a supercell, caused sporadic wind damage. This damage was associated with the rear flank downdraft of the storm. This was mainly damage to small and medium tree branches. In addition, windows were blown out on the top of the rotunda of the Texas Capitol building and an eight inch diameter tree trunk was split on the north plaza of the Capitol grounds. Maximum gusts were estimated at 65 mph.
